book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

chapters.file: ch21 - 10. And the Rest Is Drag.md
chapters.relation: Oliver Norman takes RuPaul's lyric 'we're all born naked and the rest is drag' from 'Born Naked' and asks whether its claim that everyone does drag all the time contradicts a show that crowns one drag superstar. Through Judith Butler's Gender Trouble and 'Gender is Burning' he reads drag as a play on gender that can either parody the male/female binary or reinforce it (the Mary Cheney misogyny charge, Michelle Visage's 'show woman not boy' critique, fishy queens like Courtney Act and trans queens like Gia Gunn). He then deploys Erving Goffman's Presentation of Self in Everyday Life: everyday social roles - the doctor's white coat, Alaska's Mae West on Snatch Game, the ideal pageant queen - are scripted performances with 'ideal types,' so the muscle-car seducer in the song is doing unwitting drag. The resolution: 'drag as ontology' is the low everyday form everyone performs, while Drag Race stages the high-art form that consciously fucks with the social script.

chapters.file: ch22 - 11. Lip Sync for Your Life.md
chapters.relation: Guilel Treiber reads the Season Ten reunion blow-up - Asia O'Hara blaming the show for letting The Vixen walk out, RuPaul insisting people must 'want to meet halfway' - as an unresolvable conflict between two value systems. The show's official 'C.U.N.T.' virtues (charisma, uniqueness, nerve, talent) are individualistic, market-driven values that professionalize drag, while the implicit 'A.S.S.E.' values (acceptance, solidarity, support, empowerment) descend from LGBTQ+ history from Stonewall and Marsha P. Johnson to ACT-UP. Using Nietzsche's On the Genealogy of Morals and its project of the 'revaluation of all values,' he argues values gain worth through conflict rather than progress, so there is no view from nowhere that settles the dispute. Miss Congeniality, the queens' revolt over Valentina's title, and Tammie Brown's clash with RuPaul show the show's magic lies in never deciding between the two - even though market pressure keeps devaluing solidarity.

chapters.file: ch23 - 12. The Importance of Being Fabulous.md
chapters.relation: Holly Onclin asks whether female impersonation is essential to the art of being a drag queen, testing the folk definition against Drag Race cases like Sasha Velour's bald head, Milk's goatee, the 'Bearded and Beautiful' runway, and the Season Ten super-macho 'Trade' photoshoot. Borrowing the statue-and-clay argument from Judith Jarvis Thomson and L.A. Paul, she argues a drag queen is no more identical to her conventionally feminine attributes than a statue is identical to its clay, so a queen survives losing wigs, padding, and femininity. Using Dominic Lopes's buck-passing theory of art and Peter van Inwagen's point that folk concepts are strictly inaccurate (the sun doesn't literally 'rise'), she classifies drag queens as works in the art of being a drag queen, with female impersonation a contingent convention like paper in origami. Via Kendall Walton's make-believe analysis of representation, she concludes the constant in all drag - from Snatch Game to butch male realness - is the impersonation of celebrity itself, making every queen an Oscar Wilde-style celebrity figure.

chapters.file: ch24 - Category Is … Learning from the Queens.md

chapters.relation: Anna Marie Fennell reads RuPaul's 'If you can't love yourself, how in the hell you gonna love somebody else?' through theories of self-love. Erich Fromm's four elements of love and Buddhist non-attachment (Jinkx Monsoon's 'water off a duck's back,' the Season Ten Inner Saboteur characters like Eureka's Eufilthior) ground the claim that self-love precedes healthy love for others. Against Aristophanes' myth in Plato's Symposium - the round beings split by Zeus, forever seeking their other half, retold in Hedwig and the Angry Inch - she sides with Ru: completion comes from within, not from a soulmate. Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity (the sub-man and nihilist archetypes seen in self-sabotaging queens like Nina Bo'Nina Brown) and bell hooks's All About Love with Branden's six pillars of self-esteem map onto winners like Jinkx, Sharon Needles, Violet Chachki, and Bianca Del Rio, whose drag personas show existence preceding essence.

chapters.file: ch26 - 14. You Want Some Privacy You Better Work.md
chapters.relation: Alice Fox argues that identity is self-generated, dynamic, and self-disclosing, so algorithmic 'blackbox personas' that infer traits users never disclosed - like her Boris scenario, where Grindr ads could out a closeted Drag Race fan to his conservative family - wrongly override self-identified identity and enable stereotyping, election manipulation, and persecution of LGBTQ+ people. Drawing on Giorgio Agamben's 'ethical spaces' from Nudities and Samuel von Pufendorf's duty to protect fellow humans ('benefits par excellence'), she claims a moral responsibility to defend everyone's personas against surveillance capitalism, since institutions will not. Drag Race supplies the training manual: queens' mastery of persona creation and transformation - Kim Chi vs Sang-Young Shin, Alaska vs Justin Honard, Snatch Game's celebrity personae that defeat even facial recognition - teaches obfuscation, consistency, and fluidity (Finstas, ad blockers, varied routines) so algorithms cannot tell the authentic from the gag.

Carolina Are examines the Facebook group Fire WERK With Me, where fans mash up Drag Race and Twin Peaks, as a 'sub-subculture' whose memes, shade, and catchphrases ('Miss Vanjie,' 'Stop relying on that body' aimed at Laura Palmer's body) only double insiders can decode. She argues that the show's diffusion of drag language from Paris Is Burning, its meta-commentary on reality-TV formats like America's Next Top Model, and the Doppelganger motif shared with Lynch's show (drag queen in and out of drag vs good and evil Agent Cooper) exemplify meta-reality and convergence culture: fans become producers whose meme creation co-authors the shows' meaning. The group's 'meta-shade' - such as Alyssa Edwards's 'Girl, look how orange you fucking look' read redirected at Kyle MacLachlan's tanned evil Doppelganger - shows online fandom as performative, educational interpretation rather than trolling.

Hendrik Kempt reads Drag Race's pervasive death imagery - death-drops, the 'lip sync for your life,' mirror messages, the 'Death Becomes Her' runway - through the philosophy of death. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' and Stoic self-possession (Ru's 'pay them bitches no mind,' Violet Chachki enduring a tiny corset) explain why elimination, like death, gives no ground for worry once it arrives, while Socrates' 'philosophy is training for death' makes the show a workout video for dying - Socrates even dying fussing over a rooster like a drag mother to Miss Fame. Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death set up Sartre's radically free, future-oriented self - so voluntary exits like BenDeLaCreme's self-elimination and Charlie Hides's listless lip-sync betray one's own plans - and Camus's Sisyphus makes Chi Chi DeVayne and Roxxxy Andrews's doomed All Stars returns models of 'acceptance without resignation.' The closing weighs transhumanism's promise of conquered death against a DragCon-forever thought experiment, concluding with Ru's roast eulogy for Lady Bunny that love and irreverence, not immortal life, are the point.

chapters.file: ch30 - Trading Cards Philosophers as Drag Queens.md

holes.name: Erving Goffman
holes.what: Sociologist whose The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life analyzes all social interaction as theatrical performance with roles, scripts, fronts, and idealizations.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Goffman's performance and 'ideal type' framework as its main lens for reading 'Born Naked,' Snatch Game, and pageant-queen personae.

holes.name: Revaluation of All Values (genealogy)
holes.what: Nietzsche's project in On the Genealogy of Morals of asking how values gained their worth through conflict, and of creating new values in their re-evaluation.
holes.why: Chapter 22 frames the entire C.U.N.T.-vs-A.S.S.E. value conflict of Drag Race through Nietzsche's revaluation and genealogical method, neither of which has a taxonomy slug.

holes.name: What Is Art? (art status and the avant-garde)
holes.what: The philosophy-of-art debate over what makes something a work of art, from Danto's and Dickie's theories to Lopes's buck-passing theory and Walton's make-believe.
holes.why: Chapter 23's core question - whether a drag queen is a work of art and what the characteristic practice of her art form is - rests entirely on art-status theory the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Material Constitution (the statue and the clay)
holes.what: The metaphysical argument that a thing and its matter can coincide without being identical, as a statue depends on but is not the clay constituting it.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses the statue-and-clay argument to show a drag queen survives losing every conventionally feminine attribute, so female impersonation is not essential to drag.

holes.name: Erich Fromm
holes.what: Humanistic psychoanalyst and social philosopher whose The Art of Loving defines love as an active practice of care, responsibility, respect, and knowledge.
holes.why: Chapter 25 builds its whole account of self-love before loving others on Fromm's four elements of love and his having-vs-being contrast.

holes.name: Giorgio Agamben
holes.what: Contemporary Italian philosopher of bio-politics and 'bare life' whose Nudities describes 'ethical spaces' for reflecting between performances.
holes.why: Chapter 26 borrows Agamben's 'ethical spaces' as its central framing for the privacy between personas that digital surveillance destroys.

holes.name: Samuel von Pufendorf
holes.what: Seventeenth-century natural-law theorist of the duty of man and citizen, including duties owed to humanity at large.
holes.why: Chapter 26 rests its call to protect fellow humans from algorithmic surveillance on Pufendorf's 'benefits par excellence' duty to humanity.

holes.name: Privacy and Surveillance
holes.what: The political problem of protecting self-generated identity and personal data from institutional, corporate, or algorithmic surveillance and profiling.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire argument is that blackbox data personas override self-identified identity and that Drag Race-style masking practices are needed to protect privacy.

holes.name: Convergence Culture (participatory fandom)
holes.what: Media-theory account in which digital fan communities become subcultures of producers whose participation and content creation shape how shows operate.
holes.why: Chapter 27 explains Fire WERK With Me's memes and the Drag Race fandom's co-creation of the show through subculture and convergence-culture theory the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Meta-Reality and Media Meta-Commentary
holes.what: Roy Bhaskar and Jamie Morgan's notion of realities 'beyond reality as currently understood,' applied to television that comments on and parodies itself.
holes.why: Chapter 27 uses meta-reality and meta-commentary as its main analytic frame for Drag Race as a 'meta' show and its Twin Peaks meme crossover group.

holes.name: Transhumanism
holes.what: The movement holding that death is a disease technology may eventually cure, making radical life extension and the abolition of death a goal.
holes.why: Chapter 28's closing section weighs the transhumanist demand to abolish death against a DragCon-eternity thought experiment showing endless life sours enjoyment.
